title: IBM and Rutgers Control Quantum Chaos Across 100 Qubits on Heron Processor - Quantum Computing Report
author: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
text:
Researchers from Rutgers University, IBM Quantum, and collaborating academic institutions have demonstrated real-time quantum feedback control across 100 qubits on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron superconducting processor (`ibm_fez`). Published in Nature Physics, the study implements adaptive quantum circuits that interleave entangling gates with mid-circuit measurements and resets, providing experimental validation of non-unitary dynamics critical for scalable quantum error correction (QEC).

The experiment executed nearly 5,000 two-qubit entangling gates and nearly 5,000 mid-circuit measurement-based resets across 100 linearly connected qubits. By stochastically competing information-scrambling operations (a quantum analog of the classically chaotic Bernoulli map) against local resets pushing qubits toward the zero state, the team observed and characterized a dynamical control-induced phase transition (CIPT) between chaotic volume-law and controlled unentangled phases.

Quantum Fluctuation Sampling and Hardware Certification

To distinguish true coherent quantum dynamics from classical noise, the researchers measured the variance of shot-to-shot quantum fluctuations (varQ[Mz]) across 10,000 shots per circuit configuration. Comparing experimental distributions against classical dephasing Markov models using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence confirmed that the processor sampled a genuine quantum random process rather than purely incoherent stochastic noise.

The study marks one of the largest experimental realizations of real-time feedback and non-unitary adaptive circuits to date, validating theoretical matrix product state (MPS) models and statistical mechanics mappings on physical hardware.
